lesson.title: Who gains from a sale

steps.headline: Surplus is the gap between a limit and the price actually paid.

lead.text: Each point on the demand curve is the most some buyer would pay: their willingness to pay. Consumer surplus is that amount minus the price paid. Producer surplus is the seller's version: the price received minus the lowest price they would accept.

reveal.text: The gap is value she kept: her consumer surplus. Add up every buyer's gap and you get an area on the diagram.

lead.text: Take one buyer in the coffee market, where every cup sells at the same market price.

steps.headline: Bagels: Qd = 90 − 3P and Qs = 2P − 10. Find consumer surplus.

workedSteps.text: Find the equilibrium price and quantity.
Find the price at which demand reaches zero.
The base is the quantity sold; the height is the gap between that price and the market price.
Take half of base times height.

steps.headline: Coffee sells 60 cups at £20, with Qd = 100 − 2P and Qs = 4P − 20. Find both surpluses.

workedSteps.text: Demand reaches zero at £50, so the buyers' height is the gap above the price.
Half of base times height gives consumer surplus.
Supply starts at £5, so the sellers' height is the gap below the price.
Half of base times height gives producer surplus.

reveal.text: Same moves: equilibrium, the price where demand reaches zero, then half of base times height.

lead.text: A different market, the same triangle. Find the market price first.

steps.headline: Free exchange at equilibrium makes total surplus as large as it can be.

lead.text: Total surplus is consumer surplus plus producer surplus. A cup adds to it when its buyer values it above its cost to make. Equilibrium trades every such cup and no other.

reveal.text: The lost value is the triangle of base 20 and height 15: £150 of deadweight loss, surplus that nobody gets.

lead.text: Now a rule caps coffee sales below the free-market quantity. The cups that can no longer be sold are the ones to look at.

lesson.orientation: Measure consumer and producer surplus as areas on the diagram and see why equilibrium makes their total largest.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Three friends each have a limit on what they would pay for a concert ticket.

intro.promise: By the end you'll measure who gains from a sale as areas on the diagram, and show why equilibrium makes the total largest.

recap.keyIdea: Consumer surplus is the gap between what buyers would pay and the price. Producer surplus is the gap between the price and what sellers would accept. Equilibrium makes their total as large as possible.

blocks.text: You found £900 of consumer surplus and £450 of producer surplus in the coffee market. Capping sales at 40 cups wasted £150 of it.

recap.nextHook: What happens to that surplus when a tax drives a wedge between buyers and sellers?

questions.prompt: A buyer would pay up to £35 for a cup of coffee and buys it at the market price of £20. How much consumer surplus does she gain, in pounds?
hints: Consumer surplus is the gap between willingness to pay and the price paid.
Start from her maximum, not from the price.
Subtract the price from her maximum.
questions.onCorrect: £15. Willingness to pay minus the price paid is the surplus on that cup.

misconceptions.feedback: That is her maximum. Surplus is the part she did not have to pay.
That is the price. Surplus is the gap between her maximum and the price.
Adding them does not measure a gap. Subtract.

hints: Consumer surplus is a triangle above the price and below the demand curve.
Its height runs from the price up to the price at which demand reaches zero.
Take one half × base × height, with the quantity sold as the base.
questions.onCorrect: £900. Half of base times height: the 60 cups sold, and the 30 between price and top of the demand curve.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the half. A triangle's area is half of base times height.
That is the base only. Find the area.

hints: Producer surplus is a triangle below the price and above the supply curve.
Its height runs from the lowest supply price up to the market price.
Take one half × quantity × that height.
questions.onCorrect: £450. Half of the 60 cups sold times the 15 between the lowest supply price and the market price.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the half. A triangle's area is half of base times height.
That is the height only. Find the area.

questions.prompt: A rule caps coffee sales at 40 cups, below the free-market 60. For the 40th cup, buyers would pay £30 and sellers would accept £15. By how many pounds does total surplus fall?
hints: The lost units run from the 40th up to the 60th.
On each lost unit the loss is the gap between what buyers would pay and what sellers would accept.
Those gaps form a triangle, so take one half × base × height.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The lost cups form a triangle with base 60 − 40 = 20 and height 30 − 15 = 15: ½ × 20 × 15 = £150.

questions.onCorrect: £150. The cups that no longer sell were each worth more to buyers than they cost sellers.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the half. A triangle's area is half of base times height.
That is only the height of the lost triangle. Find its area.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 80 − 2P and supply is Qs = 2P. What is consumer surplus at equilibrium, in pounds?
hints: Find the equilibrium price and quantity first.
Find the price at which quantity demanded falls to zero.
Take one half × quantity × (that price minus the equilibrium price).

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 80 − 2P = 2P gives P = £20 and Q = 40. Demand reaches zero at £40, so CS = ½ × 40 × (40 − 20) = £400.

questions.onCorrect: £400. Find the market price and quantity first, then take half of base times height.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the half. A triangle's area is half of base times height.
That is the market price, not the area.
Check the height: it runs from the market price up to where demand reaches zero.

questions.prompt: Which area on a supply and demand diagram is consumer surplus?
hints: Consumer surplus belongs to buyers, so look for the curve that records buyers' values.

acceptedIdeas: Below the demand curve and above the price, up to the quantity sold
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Buyers gain the gap between what they would pay and the price they do pay. The demand curve records what they would pay.

choices.label: Below the demand curve and above the price, up to the quantity sold
Above the supply curve and below the price, up to the quantity sold
Below the supply curve, up to the quantity sold

questions.onCorrect: Buyers gain the gap between what they would pay and what they pay: below the demand curve, above the price.

misconceptions.feedback: That area belongs to sellers: it sits above the supply curve.
Below the supply curve is the cost of production, not a gain.

questions.prompt: Three friends would pay up to £30, £25 and £20 for a ticket. Tickets cost £22. Together, how many pounds better off are the friends who buy?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first two buy: (30 − 22) + (25 − 22) = 8 + 3 = 11. The third would pay only 20, so does not buy.

hints: Who is willing to pay at least the price?
For each buyer, how far above the price is their limit?
Add those gaps for the buyers only.
questions.onCorrect: £11. Each buyer gains the gap between what they would pay and the price. The third friend does not buy, so adds nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds up what they would pay. Only the gap above the price counts.
The third friend would not buy at that price, so there is no loss to subtract.

choices.label: It runs from the price paid up to the highest price anyone would pay.

acceptedIdeas: It runs from the price paid up to the highest price anyone would pay.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Demand reaches zero at £30, and the price is £20. The surplus sits between them.

hints: Where does the surplus sit on the price axis?
questions.onCorrect: Surplus sits between the price paid and the top of the demand curve.

misconceptions.feedback: Quantity is on the other axis. The height is measured in pounds.
Buyers pay the market price. The 30 is the most anyone would pay.

questions.prompt: A cup beyond the equilibrium quantity is worth £18 to its buyer and costs £22 to make. Would selling it raise total surplus?

choices.label: No: it costs more than it is worth.
Yes: someone is willing to buy it.
Yes: the seller makes a profit.

acceptedIdeas: No: it costs more than it is worth.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The cup adds £18 of value and uses £22 of cost, so total surplus would fall by £4.

hints: Compare the value the buyer gets with the cost of making it.
questions.onCorrect: No. A trade raises total surplus only if the buyer's value exceeds the seller's cost.

misconceptions.feedback: Willingness to buy at some price is not enough. The buyer's value has to exceed the cost of making it.
At a price above the buyer's value no sale happens. At a price they will pay, the seller loses on the cup.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 100 − 5P and supply is Qs = 5P. What is consumer surplus at equilibrium, in pounds?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 − 5P = 5P gives P = £10 and Q = 50. Demand reaches zero at £20. CS = ½ × 50 × (20 − 10) = £250.

hints: Find the equilibrium price and quantity first.
Find the price at which demand reaches zero.
Take half of the quantity times the gap between that price and the market price.
questions.onCorrect: £250. Equilibrium first, then half of base times height.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the half. A triangle's area is half of base times height.
That is the market price, not the area.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 80 − 4P and supply is Qs = 4P − 16. What is producer surplus at equilibrium, in pounds?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 80 − 4P = 4P − 16 gives P = £12 and Q = 32. Supply starts at £4. PS = ½ × 32 × (12 − 4) = £128.

hints: Find the equilibrium price and quantity first.
Find the price below which sellers offer nothing.
Take half of the quantity times the gap between the market price and that price.
questions.onCorrect: £128. Half of the quantity sold times the gap above the lowest supply price.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the half. A triangle's area is half of base times height.
That is the market price, not the area.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 100 − 5P and supply is Qs = 5P, so 50 units sell at £10. A cap limits sales to 40. At the 40th unit buyers would pay £12 and sellers would accept £8. By how many pounds does total surplus fall?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The lost units form a triangle: base 50 − 40 = 10, height 12 − 8 = 4. ½ × 10 × 4 = £20.

hints: Which units are no longer traded?
What is the gap between buyers' value and sellers' cost at the 40th unit?
The lost surplus is a triangle: take half of base times height.
questions.onCorrect: £20. The units that cannot be sold were each worth more to buyers than they cost sellers.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the half. A triangle's area is half of base times height.
That is the base only. Find the area.

citations.claim: Surplus is the gap between a limit and the price actually paid. Each point on the demand curve is the most some buyer would pay: their willingness to pay. Consumer surplus is that amount minus the price paid. Producer surplus is the seller's version: the price received minus the lowest price they would accept.
Take one buyer in the coffee market, where every cup sells at the same market price. The gap is value she kept: her consumer surplus. Add up every buyer's gap and you get an area on the diagram.
Bagels: Qd = 90 − 3P and Qs = 2P − 10. Find consumer surplus.
Coffee sells 60 cups at £20, with Qd = 100 − 2P and Qs = 4P − 20. Find both surpluses.
A different market, the same triangle. Find the market price first. Same moves: equilibrium, the price where demand reaches zero, then half of base times height.

Free exchange at equilibrium makes total surplus as large as it can be. Total surplus is consumer surplus plus producer surplus. A cup adds to it when its buyer values it above its cost to make. Equilibrium trades every such cup and no other.

Now a rule caps coffee sales below the free-market quantity. The cups that can no longer be sold are the ones to look at. The lost value is the triangle of base 20 and height 15: £150 of deadweight loss, surplus that nobody gets.
The lost cups form a triangle with base 60 − 40 = 20 and height 30 − 15 = 15: ½ × 20 × 15 = £150.
80 − 2P = 2P gives P = £20 and Q = 40. Demand reaches zero at £40, so CS = ½ × 40 × (40 − 20) = £400.
Buyers gain the gap between what they would pay and the price they do pay. The demand curve records what they would pay.
The first two buy: (30 − 22) + (25 − 22) = 8 + 3 = 11. The third would pay only 20, so does not buy.
Demand reaches zero at £30, and the price is £20. The surplus sits between them.
The cup adds £18 of value and uses £22 of cost, so total surplus would fall by £4.
100 − 5P = 5P gives P = £10 and Q = 50. Demand reaches zero at £20. CS = ½ × 50 × (20 − 10) = £250.
80 − 4P = 4P − 16 gives P = £12 and Q = 32. Supply starts at £4. PS = ½ × 32 × (12 − 4) = £128.
The lost units form a triangle: base 50 − 40 = 10, height 12 − 8 = 4. ½ × 10 × 4 = £20.
50 − P = P − 10 gives P = £30 and Q = 20. Sellers offer nothing below £10, so PS = ½ × 20 × (30 − 10) = £200.
